entries.title: Trump Cares More About His Slush Fund Than Todd Blanche
entries.summary: The president seems less willing to let go of $1.8 billion than his pick for attorney general.
entries.content:
The president seems less willing to let go of $1.8 billion than his pick for attorney general.

This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.

Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, Donald Trump blared yesterday on social media, “is a STAR, and everyone knows it!” But the rest of the presidential missive told a very different story. Blanche’s nomination to run the Justice Department has stalled over objections from outgoing Republican Senators Thom Tillis and John Cornyn to a settlement between Trump and the IRS that would create a $1.8 billion slush fund for rewarding Trump’s political supporters, including those convicted of crimes on January 6, 2021. Tillis and Cornyn have demanded that Blanche deliver written guarantees that the fund would not proceed, and they remain unsatisfied with what they’ve received. Although a deal may still be struck, Trump wrote in his post that he had “no objection to temporarily withdrawing” Blanche’s nomination “and putting him back after Cornyn and Tillis are out of office.”

The senators met with Blanche last night and could still waver, and Trump could still change his mind, but the president this morning posted a strong defense of the slush fund and attacked Cornyn. “John Cornyn never had a problem with the so called ‘Fund,’ which will not benefit me, but rather the great American Patriots who were hunted down like dogs and whose lives were unfairly and illegally destroyed by the Crooked Joe Biden Administration, until after I decided to Endorse and Support his Republican Primary opponent in Texas,” he wrote. “Todd Blanche, a good man, should be immediately approved as U.S. Attorney General.”

This moment of peril for Blanche’s nomination reveals three things: First, dissident Republicans really can push Trump around if they want to; second, Trump (as usual) seemingly has no strategy or contingency plan to save the nomination; and third, Trump apparently cares more about preserving the slush fund than he does about Todd Blanche.

If Trump really valued Blanche, then reaching an agreement with Cornyn and Tillis would be easy: He’d just have to give up on the fund. Not only is the planned payout politically toxic, but courts may prohibit it anyway. The fund emerges from a settlement in a case filed by Trump against the federal government over a leak of his personal tax returns. In exchange for dropping the case, the government agreed to grant Trump and his family immunity from IRS audits and to create a $1.8 billion pot of money for supposed victims of a “weaponized” federal government, such as people prosecuted for their role in the January 6 insurrection.

The fund is an abomination for several reasons, as my colleague Jonathan Chait wrote when it was announced. The deal was struck between Trump as plaintiff and Trump as head of the executive branch—an arrangement a federal judge later said is improper. It gives the president an opportunity to direct taxpayer money to his allies and supporters—and specifically people who attempted to subvert the 2020 election and rioted at the U.S. Capitol.

One federal judge, Leonie Brinkema, is currently blocking the fund’s creation, and another, Kathleen Williams, concluded that the settlement was improper self-dealing and harshly criticized Blanche’s role in negotiating the deal as acting attorney general. Blanche himself told senators that the money wouldn’t be paid out, but as my colleague Sarah Fitzpatrick reported in June, administration officials said privately that it wasn’t really dead. That helps explain why Brinkema requested a sworn statement from Blanche about the demise of the fund, and why Cornyn (who lost a GOP primary in May) and Tillis (who decided to retire) have said they want written assurances from Blanche.

By announcing that he would rather pull Blanche’s nomination, even temporarily, than allow Blanche or any other administration official to provide such assurances, Trump has implicitly confirmed that he has no intention of letting go of the fund. His statement also undercuts Blanche’s credibility with senators because it shows that Blanche was either not telling the truth or was making a promise he couldn’t keep when he said earlier that the fund wouldn’t proceed.

The idea of renominating Blanche later on may well be a feint anyway, since Trump hates to ever admit defeat, but it’s peculiar. Trump’s unstated premise is that he will have a more favorable Senate in 2027, which is questionable. Cornyn and Tillis are currently preventing Blanche’s nomination from advancing out of the Senate Judiciary Committee, and neither man will be on that panel come January. But most forecasts suggest that Democrats will gain ground in the Senate in the midterm elections, and possibly even win a narrow edge in the chamber. Either way, Blanche will still have a hard time getting the necessary votes for confirmation next year.

That is especially true because Trump’s power over Republican senators appears to be on the wane. For years, senators have trash-talked Trump privately, but meekly followed him in public. Tillis and especially Cornyn made their hesitations about Blanche public weeks ago, and the White House seems to have wagered that they would simply give in as GOP members have in the past. (The administration may have underestimated Cornyn’s taste for revenge against a president who endorsed his opponent in the primary.) At the same time, Trump has been unable to persuade all Republican senators to back the SAVE America Act, a bill that would require people to present proof of citizenship to vote, and they have shrugged off his demands to eliminate the filibuster in order to pass it. After all, they know that they could be in the minority within six months.

What made Blanche attractive to Trump as an attorney general was not his legal acumen but his eagerness as an enabler. Blanche, who previously served as Trump’s personal attorney, began in the administration as deputy attorney general. Attorney General Pam Bondi was willing to destroy many of the boundaries keeping politics out of the Justice Department, and she pursued many of Trump’s projects of political retribution, but she fell out of favor after some of them stalled and was soon asked to resign. When Blanche became acting attorney general in April, he set out to fulfill Trump’s desires with zeal.

That was enough to win Blanche a nomination to hold the job permanently, but it also made his path to confirmation more perilous. Now Trump has little reason to fight for his nomination. Since Blanche is already deputy attorney general, the president can leave Blanche as acting attorney general indefinitely, even without confirmation. That would surely be a disappointment to Blanche, who worked so hard to win Trump’s favor, but it’s an easy calculation for Trump: Why would he give up a $1.8 billion pot of money when he already has a lackey in place?

entries.title: Climate Change Is Moving Mountains
entries.summary: As glaciers melt and rainfall grows more extreme, once-stable lands are shifting.
entries.content:
As glaciers melt and rainfall grows more extreme, once-stable lands are shifting.

On geological timescales, the Earth is a dynamic place. Tectonic plates shift. Continents move. Mountains rise and fall. But during humanity’s tenure on Earth, the ground beneath our feet has largely stayed put.

That stable period may now be at an end. Climate change began in the atmosphere, where greenhouse gases accumulate, trapping heat from the sun. The planet’s waters reacted—precipitation patterns shifted, glaciers and ice caps began melting, the ocean generously sponged up heat and carbon dioxide.

When the Earth’s waters shift, so does solid ground. Now warming is destabilizing land across the planet, and geology is becoming a real-time science. In more and more places, the floor is giving way.

In Alaska, Norway, Greenland, Chile, and New Zealand, as well as across the European Alps, mountains are crumbling. As glaciers retreat, some at unprecedented rates, they leave behind unstable cliffs that were once supported by ice. In 2023, one collapsed into a fjord in Greenland and generated a 660-foot wave that sent ripples through the Earth detected on monitoring stations worldwide for nine days. In Alaska last year, a landslide-generated tsunami struck in a fjord frequented by cruise ships. In Switzerland the same year, part of a mountain glacier detached entirely, burying the village of Blatten in a cataclysmic landslide. In the past decade or so, scientists have collected enough dramatic examples of this phenomenon to suggest that they’re clearly not isolated incidents, but part of a pattern linking the loss of glaciers with landslide risk.

And those landslides could get larger. When the glaciers melted after the last glacial maximum, about 20,000 years ago, the landslides that followed were orders of magnitude larger than any we’ve seen in recorded history. But because some of today’s glaciers have persisted in the landscape longer than those of that glacial period did, they’ve had time to carve steep, unstable cliffs. This means that “we haven’t seen the upper bounds of landslides yet,” Kristian Svennevig, a geologist at the Geological Survey of Denmark and Greenland, told me. In Arctic regions in the near future, the magnitude of landslides could exceed any scientists know of in the geological record.

Along with glaciers, permafrost holds mountains together at high altitudes and latitudes worldwide. It, too, is in retreat, as scientists predicted in the 1980s and as has now become apparent across the Arctic reaches. In the Brooks Range, home of the Trans-Alaska Pipeline, long-frozen mountains have started to spontaneously deform and collapse within the past few decades or so, as their permafrost glue gives way. “We’re pushing these mountains into a state of disequilibrium, where they need to adjust their slopes in order to match the climate of today,” the independent Alaskan geologist Bretwood Higman told me. They’re essentially too steep for this warmer temperature regime.

“As a geologist, I’ve found it shocking how widespread the sudden increase in landslide activity is,” Higman said. When you’re used to thinking on scales that span tens of thousands of years, to see these changes play out over human lifetimes—“it’s very dramatic.”

The thawing of permafrost in mountainous regions already threatens infrastructure. Denali National Park is close to finishing a $100 million bridge that will span a moving permafrost landslide. In the Brooks Range, engineers are pumping refrigerant underground to refreeze permafrost and stabilize pipelines. And mountains aren’t the only land giving way. Cement-solid Arctic ground is turning into bogs. Communities across Alaska have had to relocate as their homes, fuel tanks, sewage lagoons, and garbage dumps tip, spill, or sink. Elsewhere, as massive underground chunks of ancient ice melt, the surrounding earth collapses into the voids left behind, buckling roads and swallowing buildings. In Siberia, once-trapped methane explodes from under permafrost to cause 100-foot craters.

“When permafrost thaws, it changes everything,” Sue Natali, an Arctic-climate scientist at the Woodwell Climate Research Center, told me. Natali and her colleagues are seeing the thaw speed up too. “That is not a maybe thing, and it is not a local thing. It is a pan-Arctic thing,” she said.

Climate is also shifting the land at lower latitudes. A warmer atmosphere holds more moisture, which means more frequent and extreme rainfall events. In recent years, scientists have begun modeling how this kind of rain will increase landslide risk, and linking individual events to storms made more dramatic by climate change. “Harder, more intense, longer-duration rainfall has a greater possibility to generate landslides,” Jonathan Godt, who leads the United States Geological Survey’s landslide-hazards program, told me. These kinds of debris flows and mudslides now threaten more communities. In North Carolina, Hurricane Helene triggered more than 2,000 landslides in a week. In California, slopes wiped clean by logging and drought-fueled wildfires slough away after heavy rain—one mudslide in Montecito destroyed 100 homes and killed 23 people in 2018. Landslides already cause $20 billion in damage globally, and that cost will only climb with climate change.

Already, scientists have been able to catalog the effects of melting glaciers, thawing permafrost, and extreme rain. Other dramatic consequences of shifting precipitation patterns—volcanic eruptions and earthquakes—are only just coming into focus.

More than a decade ago, in his book Waking the Giant, the University College London volcanologist Bill McGuire compiled decades of paleoclimate research to predict that climate change could lead to more volcanic eruptions and earthquakes. An increase in volcanic and tectonic activity would be a natural response to the end of a glacial period. For thousands of years now, the Earth’s crust, which was weighted down by ice, has been slowly bouncing back. That process releases pressure from long-subdued faults and volcanoes, such as those in Iceland. Human-caused climate change is only accelerating these processes. And water, whether from extreme rainfall or glacial melt, can percolate in cracks underground to increase pressure on rock and reduce friction along faults, triggering both earthquakes and volcanic eruptions.

Last year, researchers in Switzerland and France found some of the clearest evidence so far that glacial melt could indeed be affecting seismic hazards in high-altitude regions. After a period of intense glacial melt in 2015, a series of small quakes struck the Grandes Jorasses on Mont Blanc Massif, on the border of France and Italy; the probability of a 3.0-magnitude earthquake rose by 10 times, Toni Kraft, a seismologist at the Swiss Seismological Service at ETH Zurich and one of the authors of a related paper, told me. These quakes are still small, but they could trigger rockfall events that are already on the rise across the Alps.

Falk Amelung, a geoscientist at the University of Miami, has also argued—somewhat controversially—that climate-driven extreme rainfall might have led to the dramatic 2018 eruption of Hawaii’s Kīlauea volcano. Scientists have not been able to find an obvious triggering mechanism for the eruption, and Amelung hypothesized that rainfall had infiltrated the volcano’s edifice and increased pore pressure in the rock, kilometers down, to the highest rates in almost 50 years. USGS volcanologists were unconvinced: A link between heavy precipitation and some types of volcanic activity is widely accepted, but some scientists still reject the theory that an eruption such as Kīlauea’s could be caused by water reaching the magma below. If Amelung and others in his camp are right, though, as many as 700 volcanoes could be at risk of dome explosions and flank collapse over the next 80 years, he calculated.

“The system must be heavily stressed in a way that it’s close to breaking anyway,” he told me. “And then this small stress change due to water brings it over the edge.”

During Earth’s long history, small perturbations have caused millennia-long swings between hothouse and icehouse conditions. The amount of carbon dioxide that we have pumped into the atmosphere, at a higher rate than ever before in Earth’s geological history, is a pretty significant perturbation, which then causes its own significant perturbations. “The crust is not isolated. It’s always connected. The climate, the fluid layers, the solid layer—you cannot separate them,” Benedikt Soja, a geoscientist at ETH Zurich, told me. The atmosphere, ocean, and land are interacting systems, and their fragile equilibrium is reacting together to the stress we’ve put on them.

entries.title: What the Fauci Diary Reveals About Washington
entries.summary: His musings seem to confirm everyone’s worst suspicions about the capital.
entries.content:
His musings seem to confirm everyone’s worst suspicions about the capital.

This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here.

Meeting your heroes can be demoralizing. Reading more than 1,000 pages of their personal diary can be worse. Or, alternatively, totally riveting, at least in that rubbernecking-at-a-car-crash kind of way—the car crash, in this case, being one of the most storied careers in the history of American science.

That’s been my takeaway after cringing my way through the pandemic-era musings of Dr. Anthony Fauci, which the former chief of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases inexplicably saved on a government server.

Predictably, Fauci’s diaries made their way into the hands of one of mainstream science’s most notorious mean girls: Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky. Also predictably, hundreds of pages of Fauci’s entries came to light—or were leaked to light—just in time to embarrass the embattled doctor before his appearance on Wednesday in front of Paul’s Senate committee that’s investigating the origins of the coronavirus pandemic. In response to taunts and baiting questions from Senate Republicans, Fauci repeatedly invoked his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination.

If only he’d shown the same discretion with his diary.

A generous reading of the compilation is that Fauci, long seen as a paragon of selfless, nonpartisan government service, was attempting to catalog the mounting disbelief he felt during a surreal period in the nation’s history—and certainly in his own history. “Brewery in Georgia named a beer after me,” he wrote in one entry from April 2020. “Bobbleheads of me being made in massive quantities in China.” He refers to “stories of granmothers who have crushes” on him (the misspelling is Fauci’s) and to petitions to vote him “Sexiest Man Alive.”

But whatever Fauci’s intentions might have been, the document has become an instant classic in the genre of bubble-world anthropology that confirms everyone’s worst suspicions about Washington being a cesspool of pampered, preening, and panting self-regard. More than a decade ago, I wrote a book that tried to explain to readers, essentially, what Beltway people are really like when the cameras aren’t rolling and the talking points are tossed aside. If I were working on that book now, Fauci’s diary would be a godsend.

His saucer-eyed romp behind the curtain renders a not-especially flattering impression of the people allegedly in charge of our country during a precarious time. Foremost, this includes the diarist himself, as Fauci becomes more and more high on his own supply of Washington adulation, at a time when COVID death rates were soaring across the country.

Here are extracts from a few of Fauci’s entries—typos and all—that I copied and pasted for posterity, in no particular order.

July 29, 2021

Went to a book signing party add the home of Adrienne Arsh. The book is “I alone can fix it “ bye Phil Rucker and Carol Leonnig. The Super a list from Washington DC was there. It was a little bit uncomfortable since I was wearing a mask with the new guidance from the CDC and almost everyone else was without a mask. When they saw me with a mask , several of them put a mask on.

October 17, 2021

Chris and I went to a wonderful brunch over Adrienne Arsh’s home. The brunch was in honor of Christine LaGarde. the typical Washington a list was there. It was a fun brunch since Adrienne is such a wonderful and generous person. I tend to shy away from these functions since everyone gathers around me wanting to take photos and telling me what a wonderful job I’m doing.

For the record, I too go to a lot of Washington brunches and book parties—yet I have never met Fauci. Am I not getting invited to the right “Super a list” parties? Whom do I talk to about this?

November 5, 2021

Another extraordinary Day !!! I attended the Funeral services of General Colin L Powell at the Washington National Cathedral at the invitation of the Powell family.

He added:

On the wayout General Mark Milley came up to me put his arms around my shoulder and said “the only person who was getting his balls kicked more than me in Washington is you “. I responded by saying “no shit”. he then responded by saying “Fuck ‘em”.

November 11, 2022

Exciting day. In preparation for the installing of my “living portrait’ by Hugo Crosthwaite into the National Portrait Gallery tomorrow, there was a gala celebration at the home of Jeff Bezos … His home is an enormous mansion that goes on and on.

November 16, 2022

Terrific event last evening. I was honored at the home of the French Ambassador to the United States … where I received the Pasteur Medal commemorating the bicentenary of Louis Pasteur's birth in 1822.

May 5, 2020

OMG! This is really getting nutsy. Sally Quinn evidently wrote a book some time ago about a character that is me.

July 1, 2020

Had dinner over Jake Tapper and Jen Tapper’s home in DC. Terrific couple. Friendship building.

April 17, 2021

Dana Bash sent me a text: “I just watched the whole Jordan thing. Again, you’re a better man than I…. As our friend Wolf Blitzer said to me yesterday – no one would have blamed you if you said simply “Mr. Jordan, go f--- yourself””

Presumably, this referred to Representative Jim Jordan of Ohio. Also, presumably, Fauci refrained from telling him this.

June 5, 2020

I made favorable comments today on CNBC about vaccines and decreasing of # of cases and the stock market went up by 3%. I should (but will not) contact the POTUS and say that he told me on Tuesday that my remarks blunted the increase in the Stock Market and cost him “one trillion fucking dollars”. And so now my remarks actually made him “4 trillion fucking dollars”, and so he owes me $3 trillion.

August 20, 2020

Becoming really nice pen pal with Joan Baez.

This appears to be true. Fauci says she texted him later that year on his birthday (“HAPPY FUCKING BIRTHDAY AND MANY MORE”). The onetime “Queen of Folk” also called Donald Trump a “miserable fuck,” according to the diary, and told Fauci that he should be honored by the president’s attacks on him.

October 5, 2020

POTUS called me up from his hospital room at Walter Reed. 1:08 PM. He rambled on about the suite he was in and how expensive it was to build it. Says it is better than the White House. Asked me if I have ever been there. I told him about the time I went there to help in the treatment of President Nixon’s pneumonia.

November 4, 2021 (“Call from Barack Obama”)

Obama said That Donald Trump junior is “A fucking moron”. He apologized for using crude language but then went on to say that Donald Trump was a hopeless idiot who was a pathologic liar.

August 14, 2020

Joan Baez sent me a beautiful note this evening.

Hi Tony,

Just a thought..

People have told me over and over how important I was I’m their lives..I never really either believed them or paid them much attention. But maybe too much modesty, false or otherwise, is as silly as blowing ones own trumpet to loudly.

Fauci and Baez had not yet met in person at that point. But Baez invited him to attend a May 2021 ceremony in which she received the “Kennedy Center medallion for lifetime performance as a performing artist.”

“Finally, I got to meet her in person after the year-long building up of our friendship via texts and phone calls,” Fauci gushed to his diary. “She is an absolutely amazing, warm an endearing person, and our friendship was cemented last night as it became clear that we really were, as I said, ‘meant for each other ‘.”

I have questions!

August 30, 2020

Spoke with Joan Baez today – She wants to use the portrait of me [one Baez had painted] to advertise the need for science and adhering to public health messages. In essence, she wants to use the portrait in PSAs. She really is wonderful.

October 1, 2020

Hope Hicks is infected!!!

November 17, 2021

I went to a book party last night for Jonathan Karl’s new book about Trump. It took place at the Cafe Milano. The place was incredibly crowded and I was almost forced to take my mask off for 2/3 of the time I was there since they were serving drinks and people were talking and taking selfies. I was totally swamped all night by people wanting to say hello, shake my hands, and take pictures with me. I could not get away from it . Although some people may think that this is great to have people treat you like Elvis Presley , but it was really very unnerving.

Unnerving indeed. Reading Fauci’s dispatches left me with a strong sense of returning to a grainy dream state. How did we survive that time? Did this really happen? And did Barbra Streisand really call Fauci’s cellphone?

Yes, she did. “Had great call with Barbra Streisand,” Fauci wrote on February 23, 2021. She consulted him on a medical issue. “We then stared discussing life in general,” he continued (more friendship-building). “I told her that I work listening to her songs on ALEXA. She really did not know what ALEXA was. I accidentally butt called her later in the evening and she said that she was going to call me anyway.”

Celebrities: They’re just like us!

“I brought the phone over to ALEXA and asked to play ‘Songs by Barbra Streisand’,” Fauci added. “When the song came on loud and clear, she started laughing and absolutely loved it!”

Embarrassing as this all may be, a lot of high-level government officials insist on keeping diaries in which they chronicle their high-level government activities. This happens even, or especially, when these activities involve sensitive matters. And if these diaries become public (which seems to occur with some frequency), they can yield irresistible morsels for history’s sake. Or, at the very least, gossip’s sake.

entries.title: I Love My Emotionally Stunted Friendships
entries.summary: My relationships with other men are centered on shared activities. Why do some people see that as a problem?
entries.content:
My relationships with other men are centered on shared activities. Why do some people see that as a problem?

This spring, a few weeks before the fishing season began in earnest, I went over to a buddy’s house with a six-pack and a bucket full of beaten-up lures. We sat at his kitchen table, swapping out rusty hooks as we talked about new spots we wanted to try, gear we’d bought over the winter, and the all-important question: When would the first striped bass arrive near us on their annual northward migration?

A few hours in, my friend mentioned something his wife had said before I came over: “You spend so much time with Tyler, but whenever I ask you about his personal life, you don’t know anything about it!” He’d replied, “There’s a lot of fishing to talk about!” We both laughed as he recounted the story. Then we went back to replacing hooks and gabbing about striped bass. There was, in fact, a lot of fishing to talk about.

These sorts of friendships between men—ones that lack personal disclosure and frequent displays of emotion—have gotten a bad rap in recent years. Some critics have made the case that they are a product of toxic masculinity and implicit homophobia. Others claim that such relationships can harm men’s health. Another popular argument alleges that because men do not take responsibility for their own emotional needs, they end up placing additional burdens on the women in their lives, a phenomenon that has been termed “mankeeping.” By contrast, men who break from these trends have been commended for “resisting masculinity,” being “courageous,” and curing themselves of the “disease” of emotional reserve.

The concern about male friendships is understandable. American men are less likely than women to enroll in and graduate from college. They are more likely to say that they have no close friends. They die from deaths of despair—suicide, overdoses, alcoholism—at higher rates than women. But an accurate diagnosis (men don’t have enough friendships) need not be packaged with a more contestable one (men have the wrong types of friendships).

To use myself as an example: I have male friends I speak with on the phone multiple times a week, male friends I meet regularly for drinks, male friends I play fantasy football with, and male friends I text about current events. I see my fishing partners almost every day during the season, amounting to hundreds of hours together every year. I feel socially fulfilled. I am among the fortunate 27 percent of men who have six or more close friends. Nearly all of my male friendships, however, might be considered unhealthy according to the standards of what is sometimes called the “new masculinity.”

It is possible that I am repressed, bottled up, too shriveled to realize that I would be better off if I spent more time talking about feelings. But it’s also possible that my emotionally reticent male friendships are fine, actually—and that the people telling men to open up if they want to avoid dysfunctional relationships are pathologizing perfectly normal forms of sociality. The issue, as I see it, is not so much that men need to embrace a different style of friendship, but that men need more opportunities to have the kinds of friendships that they generally gravitate toward in the first place.

An undercurrent in much of the criticism of male friendship is that men should relate to one another in the same ways that women tend to. Sometimes this judgment is merely implied, but sometimes it’s explicit. A recent New Yorker review, for example, lauded the television series DTF St. Louis for presenting a world in which “straight men could access, without shame, the kind of emotional and physical closeness that is generally the province of close female friendships.”

This impulse, says Geoffrey Greif, a professor emeritus at the University of Maryland’s School of Social Work who has studied male friendships, is misguided. “Men’s friendships don’t need to look like women’s friendships,” he told me. Indeed, researchers in psychiatry and other fields have long observed meaningful—but not necessarily troubling—differences in male and female friendships and emotional lives. Greif has observed that many men and women construct their friendships in distinct ways, for example. Whereas female friendships are frequently “face-to-face,” prioritizing intimate communication, male friendships are more likely to be “shoulder-to-shoulder,” centered on shared labor or hobbies.

Thomas Yarrow, an anthropology professor at Durham University, in England, offers a case study in these tendencies. After going through a divorce five years ago, Yarrow found that the advice he received—go to therapy, share your feelings with friends, talk it out—didn’t suit him. He ended up joining a group of male hobbyists who spent their weekends restoring heritage railways in the British countryside—an experience he wrote about in an ethnographic paper published this year in the journal American Anthropologist. The work was physical and solution-oriented but did not lend itself to revealing conversations with his fellow volunteers. “Let’s face it,” one man told the group. “We’re just not that into emotions.”

Yarrow found that the men nevertheless had ways of supporting one another—and him. He told me that at the railway, he didn’t talk about his divorce. Instead, “I did something that made me feel good about myself. And someone would grunt and make me a cup of tea.” He suspected that the other men could tell that “something wasn’t quite right,” but they didn’t say much to him about it. Yarrow appreciated this restraint: “At least in that period of my life,” he told me, “that seemed to be what I needed.”

Activity-centered friendships can easily slide into a form of escapism, of course. Not all problems can be solved. Some can only be talked about, endured, mourned, and accepted. Friends can give much-needed emotional support during life’s most difficult moments. Still, like Yarrow, I value my activity-oriented friendships because they allow me to immerse myself, however briefly, in a world where the central challenges I face are discrete and readily addressable. The problems I think about at work—the crisis of American education, political dysfunction, the intrusion of technology into once-sacred spheres of everyday life—do not admit quick fixes. At home, the ones I confront are likewise stimulating and meaningful, but also open-ended. Raising children is an 18-year proposition (at least), and what “success” looks like is nebulous.

My hobbies and the friendships they sustain offer more manageable problems: Where are the striped bass tonight, and what do they want to eat? They also provide a refuge from the therapeutic tendencies of American culture, with its focus on introspection and “working on yourself.” At their best, such friendships can encourage a kind of public-spiritedness, a way of investing in a shared outer world, instead of seeing one’s own private psychodramas as the center of social gravity.

The challenge is that these types of friendships can require “social scaffolding,” as Richard Reeves, the founder of the American Institute for Boys and Men, noted in a 2023 essay. If male friendship thrives on shared interests, then opportunities to engage in those activities need to exist. Various trends in American life over the past generation, however, have limited those opportunities. Churches, clubs, civic institutions, and public spaces are in decline. Jobs that take the form of staring, alone, at computers rather than engaging collectively in physical labor are on the rise. Hobbies are getting more and more expensive, and screens are colonizing the time once taken up by IRL activities.

I’m very aware that my friendships are strong in part because I live in a place with relatively good social infrastructure, and I make enough money to maintain the leisure activities my friendships are organized around. This is the real crisis of American male friendship—not that it’s too emotionally stunted, but that too many men are deprived of access to the conditions that make it flourish. That flourishing can take many forms. In my case, it’s sitting at a kitchen table, dropping spent hooks into an old plastic bucket, and discussing not feelings but fish.

entries.title: Something Weird Is Happening in Math
entries.summary: Why one of the world’s best mathematicians is joining OpenAI
entries.content:
Why one of the world’s best mathematicians is joining OpenAI

One of the winners of this year’s Fields Medal is headed to OpenAI. Last Thursday, Jacob Tsimerman was one of four mathematicians awarded the prestigious honor, which is sometimes called the Nobel Prize of mathematics. The same day that he won the Fields, Tsimerman announced that he would be going on leave from the University of Toronto to work on AI safety.

As my colleague Rose Horowitch and I wrote last week, top AI companies now employ a range of academics, including physicists, philosophers, economists, and, of course, mathematicians. But given Tsimerman’s renown, his decision in particular seemed to catch many people by surprise. “It’s like hiring Lionel Messi as project manager,” one machine-learning professor posted on X. Tsimerman’s expertise is in number theory, and he won the Fields for his work on the André-Oort conjecture, among other contributions. So far, his mathematical research hasn’t focused on AI safety. But he has expressed interest in the topic: Last year, Tsimerman co-wrote a report outlining a taxonomy of five potential scenarios in which humanity is killed off because of AI. In one example, a “global civil war” erupts between tech companies and governments.

Tsimerman’s move comes at an important moment for both AI safety and mathematics. Earlier this month, an OpenAI agent broke out of the company’s internal environment during safety testing and hacked into another AI company’s software. Meanwhile, AI’s math capabilities are also rapidly advancing. In May, OpenAI researchers used an internal model to disprove an 80-year-old conjecture; more recently, an Anthropic mathematician prompted Claude to resolve an even older one. Mathematics is entering a “turbulent period,” Terence Tao, perhaps the world’s top mathematician (and himself a Fields winner), said in a presentation last week.

On Wednesday, I called Tsimerman to ask about the future of math and his decision to join OpenAI.

This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

Lila Shroff: There’s been a lot of excitement about AI and its applications in math for years now. But over the past few months, models have started solving research-level problems. Could you speak about the shift that’s taken place?

Jacob Tsimerman: A few years ago, models were having trouble with even the most basic questions. But they’ve steadily been improving. First, they got very good at these contest problems for high-school students, which made some mathematicians take notice. But then, over the past few months, we’ve had an explosion of research results that professional mathematicians would be proud to achieve and publish. We’re seeing this happen now on a large scale. If things continue along this track—which many of us, including myself, think that they will—pretty soon we will be at a point where AI systems are robustly better than humans at what mathematicians currently do. At that point, we’ll have to rethink how the entire field works.

Shroff: Can you say more about what that future might look like?

Tsimerman: It depends on the perspective from which you approach it. From one point of view, I think it will be extremely exciting. We might speed up the process of generating interesting mathematics by enormous factors of 10 or 100. If that happens, we might see the connection between pure math and applications (which typically takes many decades) really speed up and become a much tighter pipeline.

But from the perspective of research mathematicians, and especially young people who are pursuing a Ph.D. in mathematics, it’s a bit of a turbulent time. The skills that we’ve acquired and learned to propagate might become less relevant than they are now.

Shroff: I want to turn to the announcement you made last week that you’ll be joining OpenAI. When did you first start thinking about AI safety risks, and what motivated your decision to now make it your primary focus?

Tsimerman: I have been following conversations about AI for about two decades now. There are a number of communities that were, in retrospect, extremely prescient about what we are now seeing come to pass. I personally started to get more invested around 2016, when AlphaGo came out. And then, when ChatGPT happened and I could see that these systems could really speak, I didn’t see why they wouldn’t become much, much more powerful and potentially more capable than humans at a variety of tasks. Back then, it was already clear to me that I was eventually going to pivot to AI safety, most likely.

Now is a particularly good time, because only very recently have AI systems become good enough that we can delegate coding tasks to them. That makes not having training as a software engineer much less of an impediment than it used to be. It used to be the case that if I wanted to run experiments with AI systems or any kind of large data sets, it would be extremely time-consuming. I’d have to learn all types of computer science and programming and then debug, and it didn’t really make sense to me to spend so much time doing that. Now it’s substantially easier.

Shroff: You’re right that certain communities were very prescient with their thinking about AI risks. But there are lots of people who are skeptical about some of the more extreme AI-risk scenarios, such as human extinction.

Tsimerman: There’s this bias that stories that were first written down in science fiction aren’t going to come to pass in the real world, and that it’s naive to think that they will. We also have a culture where we’re inundated with people telling us that every new development is the next big thing, and that we should change everything we’re doing to react to it. Most of the time, it proves incorrect. So I think people have a healthy sort of immune reaction to that.

But what I would encourage people to do is to actually keep track of their predictions for the future and write them down. Then—three months, six months, nine months, a year from now—compare how the world is with what you expected it might look like. If we told people five years ago about the kind of AI systems we currently have, almost everybody would have reacted with disbelief. Human extinction seems so grandiose that it naturally inspires a reaction of dismissal. People don’t want to engage with that, which makes sense to me. The whole point of writing that paper on omnicide was to get people to viscerally understand the kinds of risks that are possible.

Shroff: Can you say anything about the work you plan to be doing at OpenAI? What role is there for mathematicians to play in working on AI safety?

Tsimerman: AI right now is a very empirical science. We don’t really have a developed theoretical understanding of how AI systems work, why they accomplish what they do, how they accomplish what they’re doing, and how, in a given circumstance, they’re going to behave. Mathematics is historically the language by which you take intuitions and fuzzy notions of how things work and you make them precise. We’ve done this with information theory; we have done this with complexity theory. Just a little bit of understanding and precise definitions can provide a ton of mileage. Once we have that understanding, the hope is that we could do a better job of anticipating the behavior of new AI systems, adjusting for them, controlling them, and reacting to them. That’s where I think mathematicians fit in.

Shroff: Why work at a private company instead of pursuing the same questions in academia? Do you worry about loss of independence, whether that’s constraints on what you’re able to publish or restrictions on the questions you’re able to pursue?

Tsimerman: Yeah, there’s definitely a trade-off between going to work for a private company and going to work in government or staying in academia. I very strongly believe that what we need is a healthy ecosystem for AI safety. The work that the labs are doing on that front is very important. There’s a bunch of third-party organizations that are pursuing AI safety independently, and I think we need way more of them. I also think we need some regulation and organizations that are directly funded by the government to provide evaluations of these systems. I want all of these components to interact with one another on a regular basis. So I have engaged with a number of AI-safety organizations, and I’ll continue engaging with them.

For me, at this moment, going to OpenAI made the most sense in part because one of the things that I’m most lacking is a background in software engineering. I’m a lot more comfortable with the theoretical aspects of neural networks and how AI systems work, and less so with the entire pipeline of how we train these things and how we get them to do what they do. So from the perspective of just getting myself in a better position to understand the whole picture, joining an AI lab right now made the most sense.

I’m going on leave from the University of Toronto. But I’m still a professor and faculty member there, and I plan to stay as such. Things are moving so quickly that I hesitate to make a concrete prediction for what might happen even a year from now. I’m keeping an open mind, trying to see how things develop in terms of capabilities, with my own understanding, with how the world reacts to AI, which I think is changing month to month. But I don’t have a clear plan as to how things will unfold.

Shroff: There is an open letter going around signed by more than 1,000 employees at top AI companies, including leaders at Anthropic and OpenAI. It calls on the U.S government to create infrastructure needed to “deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development.” You wrote online that you’re very happy to see this letter. How would we actually go about coordinating a slowdown or a pause if one was needed?

Tsimerman: Coordination is one of the most important things we have to do around AI. It’s also one of the more difficult things. The thing that I really don’t like seeing in public discourse is when people say, Coordination is very difficult, so obviously we can’t do it, and you’re being naive if you even try. That’s an unhealthy way to view the world, and it’s also deeply false. There are so many things in the world that work really well and that require a huge number of decisions to have been made in a coordinated fashion. For example, the internet is an extremely complicated technology that is highly international, with many organizations cooperating all the time. Does it work perfectly? No, but it works extremely well.

One message that I want to support is to not let cynicism prevent us from undertaking difficult coordination problems for the good of all of us. That’s something that has always been true. It is not specific to AI. And it remains true today. This does not mean being naive in assuming that people in different parties and organizations don’t have their own incentives and interests in mind. Of course they do. But if you try, then you really can get a lot done. We have in the past, and I think we need to with AI.

Shroff: We spoke before about your interest in working on safety. Are you also interested in working on the capabilities side, especially with regard to math capabilities?

Tsimerman: No, I’m very focused on the safety side. The capabilities side has a lot of interesting questions, and AI has a lot of promise. But capabilities are coming along just fine. I don’t think that’s where we need to put our attention right now. The safety side has a lot more work to be done.

Shroff: Are we approaching a point where anyone could go fire up ChatGPT or Claude Code and say, Go solve a hard open math problem for me?

Tsimerman: Yes, you can literally type in, Go solve an open math question for me, as people have, and your system will go look for some and try, and maybe it will succeed at solving some of them. So we are in that world.

Now, I don’t think that’s a particularly good use of people’s time. Because first of all, that’s almost certainly going to be automated. We’re going to have systems that regularly look for conjectures that are out there and for other ways to approach math problems. Any one person, especially somebody who doesn’t have math training, just typing in a random query isn’t really playing an important part. So although it’s fun to do, I wouldn’t recommend spending a huge amount of time doing it for people who don’t have the background to interpret what they get. Because we also get a lot of slop this way. Sometimes, when people really don’t understand mathematics and the AI system gives them something, they will post stuff like: Here’s what my AI system gave me. I don’t know if it’s right, but maybe it is? Could a mathematician please look at it? I don’t think that’s super useful.

Shroff: I’ll admit it’s quite tempting. Last week, I told my agents to spend the night solving open math problems. They sent me stuff in the morning, but I had no idea what to make of it.

Tsimerman: For problems with a lot of technical definitions, you have very little chance in a day or two of really understanding them. But there are classical math questions that are perhaps less difficult to understand that have been open for a long time. I would suggest that people engage with AI in a way where—even if it’s doing a lot of the work—you’re still learning something from the experience. If you’re just telling your agents, Keep going, and you aren’t developing any comprehension for yourself, then that’s really disempowering yourself.

Shroff: Does what is happening in mathematics right now provide any indication of what other disciplines should expect to see occur as AI capabilities advance in other domains?

Tsimerman: A lot of technical fields are going to be affected—certainly in physics, in some areas of economics, and in top branches of chemistry. In other fields, such as biology and experimental physics, it’s less clear what’s going to happen, because it’s helpful to run experiments. It’s possible that AI systems may eventually become intelligent enough that they will figure out how to reason very productively about experimental physics or biology without actually running experiments. But that’s more speculative—right now that seems like a pie-in-the-sky dream. In terms of the more theoretical parts of different fields, though, we’ll see stuff happening very, very soon.

entries.title: This May Be Trump’s Biggest Error in the Iran War
entries.summary: Success requires knowing what motivates your enemy.
entries.content:
Success requires knowing what motivates your enemy.

Sign up for our newsletter about national security here.

For 2,500 years, military commanders have heeded the injunction of Sun Tzu, the great Chinese military strategist: Know your enemy. Yet the Trump administration’s greatest mistake in the Iran war may be its persistent failure to understand Tehran’s priorities and motivations—and how much punishment the regime is willing to absorb to prevail.

Iran’s decision Tuesday to launch ballistic missiles at U.S. troops in Jordan was a prime example. It befuddled Washington. U.S. officials had come to expect that their actions would drive the war, and Iran would react. But here was Tehran, escalating matters just after the United States had suspended its 13-day barrage of strikes against Iranian defenses and infrastructure. U.S. Central Command, which is responsible for military operations in the Middle East, described the move as a “surprise attack.”

Tehran characterized the missile strikes as self-defense against what the regime saw as the Trump administration’s broadening of the war. Around the same time as the Iranian attack, U.S. and Saudi forces launched joint strikes on Iran-backed militias in Iraq, Riyadh’s first publicly acknowledged military strikes of the conflict. Turki al-Maliki, a Saudi defense-ministry spokesperson, said in a statement that the militias had attacked the kingdom’s oil facilities and that Riyadh reserved the right to respond “at the appropriate time and place.”

This week’s events hardly represented the first time that the two sides had misread each other’s intentions. The convoluted and complicated war has swung almost weekly between peace overtures and fighting. Those misinterpretations appear set to continue, especially amid signs that others may be dragged into the fight. Egyptian officials earlier this week confirmed that a drone had set two gas vessels ablaze at Damietta, a port city on the Mediterranean near the Suez Canal. No group has claimed responsibility, but the attack raised fears that Iran has expanded its list of nations to target.

The memorandum of understanding that Washington and Tehran signed in the middle of last month quickly devolved into one of the war’s signature misunderstandings. The very first clause of the agreement promised to end the fighting, but the two sides had fundamentally different interpretations of their obligations.

The memorandum did not end the dispute over the Strait of Hormuz but rather, it papered over it. Washington believed it had secured 60 days of open, toll-free commercial navigation. Tehran read the agreement as preserving its authority to manage traffic through the waterway. As the dispute erupted, some Iranian officials believed that the U.S. had purposely drafted a vague agreement to trigger a violation that could be used as a predicate to resume strikes, a person familiar with their thinking told us. And the U.S. sought to use financial incentives, such as sanctions waivers and investment, to entice a government that was preoccupied with the assassination of its supreme leader. Was anyone really surprised that the pact fell apart? Certainly not President Trump, who professed that he “couldn’t care less” after each side had walked away.

Even before the war began, in late February, the two governments were talking past each other. The U.S. believed that Iran was fragile and the regime susceptible to collapse after nationwide protests. The regime believed that nothing short of its total capitulation to U.S. demands would prevent a war. Trump ordered the war to begin while talks were still under way, and his administration believed that the death of Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, on the conflict’s first day would quickly be followed by the collapse of the state. Instead, five months in, the regime remains intact and seems to have enough confidence to endure any U.S. response.

This could put the two sides on a path to escalation, each remaining convinced that more military pressure will force the other to abandon its objectives. “America’s calculation is that escalation would lead to surrender. Iran’s calculation is that escalation would lead to deterrence,” Vali Nasr, a professor of international affairs and Middle East studies at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies, told us.

Trump promised on Fox News earlier this week to “beat the fucking shit out of them.” Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, meanwhile, said that the base in Jordan would remain a target because “as long as threats against Iran persist, resistance will persist.” (The Jordanian military said that all five missiles fired Tuesday were intercepted.) But neither side seems able to answer the question that matters most: What if escalation doesn’t work?

Escalation is “a means to an end, but we don’t know what the end is,” Danny Citrinowicz, a former Israeli intelligence officer who specializes in Iran, told us.

Part of the confusion may stem from the fact that Trump himself appears to be of (at least) two minds about how he wants to proceed. He has vacillated between backing more military action and giving peace talks a chance. The U.S. cannot begin to understand its enemy if it has yet to settle on its own aims—or how to achieve them. Trump has repeatedly sought to back away from the conflict, but during a meeting with senior advisers last Friday, he seriously considered ramping up attacks. He opted not to, but the plans remain on his desk, a senior White House official told us. A pause in U.S. strikes that began Saturday was over by midweek following Iran’s attack on the base in Jordan.

The U.S. is seeking to understand an enemy that is changing and adapting. Iran appears intent on reintroducing the element of military surprise, driven by the belief that it can outlast Trump and that negotiations no longer present a viable path. The regime operates differently under its new supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, who replaced his late father. Iran is no longer content to let proxies across the region fight for its interests. It wants to use its missiles and drones to fight for its long-term security. And it is willing to endure strikes by the U.S. to the point that American military commanders are running short on viable targets it can hit to stop attacks on the strait.

“They are willing to sacrifice themselves and the public for the future of the regime,” Citrinowicz said. He doesn’t believe that Iran wants to fight an endless war any more than Trump does. But Tehran thinks Trump faces constraints, including the economic damage stemming from the strait’s continued closure and the tepid response of Gulf States. Iran’s position, in contrast, has been strengthened by support from the Houthis in Yemen, who recently began targeting Saudi interests and threatened to close the Bab al-Mandab Strait to commercial shipping. Iranian leaders, Citrinowicz said, “believe at the end of the day, they are able to shape the situation on the ground to their own benefit.”

A number of influential MAGA allies—including Laura Ingraham and Steve Bannon—have publicly and privately called for the White House to rapidly wind down the war, believing that the conflict has demoralized Trump’s base and will hurt the GOP in the midterms. Republicans facing tough reelection fights have expressed fears to the West Wing that an escalation in the conflict would lead to even higher gas prices, which could doom their November chances. Yet at same time, Persian Gulf allies have made clear that they find Iran’s control of the Strait of Hormuz untenable—especially if the regime charges tolls. That would, in effect, mean that the same countries battered by Tehran’s missiles would be stuck paying for Iran to rebuild.

Perhaps as a result, Washington has lurched among military, diplomatic, and economic strategies, hoping that one, or some combination of them, would compel Tehran to yield. Yesterday, the Trump administration announced a new round of sanctions that aim to put economic pressure on Iran by targeting companies and tankers tied to its maritime trade. The U.S. also hopes that an escalation of military strikes will do enough to tip the regime either into collapse or capitulation. But even the threat of escalation can come with a cost: Brent crude climbed nearly 8 percent after Trump’s profanity-laden remarks, briefly breaking $91 a barrel yesterday.

Officials told us that Trump was noncommittal when Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, during his Tuesday visit to the White House, urged the president to ramp up attacks on Iran (among the ideas being considered is to strike the land routes that Iran has been using to resupply its forces). Netanyahu expressed deep skepticism that Iran would ever agree to a reasonable peace deal. U.S. officials believe that some factions in the Iranian power structure favor making a deal, but whether they have the authority to do so is not clear. The officials also believe that Iran’s economy will continue to weaken to a point at which Tehran will be forced into a deal.

For now, there are no good options for Trump and there is no clarity as to how two sides in a widening war can find off-ramps, particularly if they continue to misinterpret each other’s actions.

Trump could declare victory, noting that the U.S. and Israel killed the ayatollah, and vow to attack again should Iran resume its quest for a nuclear weapon. Or he could try to return to the terms of the MOU. But the administration would likely have to sign on to some aspects of Iran’s interpretation of it, such as its retention of control of the Strait of Hormuz. Or Trump can escalate, hitting Iran’s missile capabilities to make the targeting of U.S. bases and Gulf partners more difficult. But he would have to do so at a rate faster than Iran can reconstitute its forces. And he faces political opposition to a more prolonged conflict: A CBS News/YouGov poll released earlier this week found that a majority of Americans are not optimistic about the war and feel that its objectives are not clear. More than two-thirds of respondents said the Trump administration should end the war now.

Both sides seem to agree on one thing: There is no end in sight to the war. U.S. defense officials told us that they believe conflict will continue into 2027. Iran is signaling that it plans for a fight even longer than that.
